## What is vulnerable

- This affects CA Unified Infrastructure Management, also known as Nimsoft or UIM, in versions 20.1, 20.3.x, and 9.20 and below.
- CA UIM is an infrastructure monitoring platform used to manage and monitor IT environments.
- The flaw is in the robot (controller) component, which is the agent that runs on monitored systems to carry out management tasks.
- The vulnerability is an improper ACL (access control list) handling issue, meaning the software does not correctly enforce rules about who is allowed to perform actions on the system.

## How it can be exploited

- The attack vector is NETWORK, so an attacker can reach the vulnerable component remotely without needing to be on the same machine.
- No login credentials and no user interaction are required, so anyone who can reach the service over the network can attempt the attack.
- Confidentiality, integrity, and availability are all rated HIGH, meaning an attacker could read data from, write data to, or execute commands on the target system.
- The CVSS score of 9.8 reflects the combination of remote access, no authentication, and full impact across all three areas.

## What action to take

- Check whether any CA Unified Infrastructure Management deployment is running version 20.1, 20.3.x, or 9.20 and below.
- Broadcom (which now owns CA Technologies) has published a security notice with remediation guidance, linked in the references below.
- Review the Broadcom security advisory and the associated technical documentation for the recommended update or patch.
- The Packet Storm reference provides additional technical background but should be treated as a third-party resource rather than an official fix.

- Confidentiality, integrity and availability are all rated HIGH, so an attacker could read sensitive data, alter device configuration or disrupt the charging station's operation.

- Check whether any Waybox Enel X charging stations are deployed and whether their web management interfaces are reachable on the local network.
- Review the vendor security bulletin linked below for specific remediation steps and any firmware updates that address this issue.

## What is vulnerable

- The attack vector is ADJACENT_NETWORK, meaning the attacker must be on the same local network segment or a directly connected network rather than attacking from the open internet.
- No login credentials and no user interaction are needed, so anyone with adjacent network access can attempt the attack without prior privileges.
- A successful exploit creates a reverse shell with administrator privileges on the DBSec server, which means the attacker gains full remote command-line control over the server.
- Confidentiality, integrity and availability are all rated HIGH, so the attacker could read, modify or delete data and disrupt the service entirely.

## What action to take

- Check whether any McAfee Database Security installation is running a version earlier than 4.8.2.
- Update to version 4.8.2 or later, as described in the vendor advisory linked below.
- Restrict network access to the DBSec server so that only trusted systems on the local network can reach it, reducing the pool of potential attackers while the update is applied.

## What is vulnerable

- This affects Apache HTTP Server, one of the most widely used web servers, in versions 2.4.49 and 2.4.50 only.
- The vulnerability is a path traversal flaw, which means an attacker can craft a URL that tricks the server into accessing files outside the directories it is supposed to serve.
- This issue exists because a previous fix for a related vulnerability (CVE-2021-41773) in version 2.4.50 was incomplete and did not fully close the path traversal route.
- If CGI scripts (programs the server can run on behalf of a visitor) are enabled for the affected paths, the flaw can also allow an attacker to run arbitrary code on the server.

## How it can be exploited

- The attack vector is NETWORK and requires no login and no user interaction, so anyone who can reach the server over the internet can attempt it without credentials.
- The attacker sends a specially crafted URL to the server that bypasses directory restrictions set by Alias-like directives, which are configuration rules that map URLs to specific folders on disk.
- If the server's configuration does not explicitly deny access to files outside the intended directories (using the "require all denied" default), the attacker can read those files.
- When CGI execution is also enabled on those paths, the attacker can go beyond reading files and execute commands on the server, giving full control over confidentiality, integrity and availability.

## What action to take

- Check whether any Apache HTTP Server instance is running version 2.4.49 or 2.4.50, as no other versions are affected.
- Upgrade to a version later than 2.4.50 as described in the Apache HTTP Server security page listed in the references.
- Review your server configuration to ensure that directories outside the intended document root have "require all denied" set, and that CGI execution is not enabled on paths that do not need it.
- Consult the vendor advisory and the distribution-specific advisories from Fedora, Gentoo, Oracle, Cisco and NetApp listed below for platform-specific upgrade guidance.

## What is vulnerable

- This affects ExifTool, a widely used command-line utility for reading and writing metadata in image and other media files, from version 7.44 onwards.
- The flaw is in how ExifTool processes the DjVu file format, which is a format designed for scanned documents and images.
- User-supplied data inside a DjVu file is not properly sanitised before being processed, which means crafted content in the file can be treated as executable instructions.
- This allows arbitrary code execution, meaning an attacker can run whatever commands they choose on the system that parses the malicious file.

## How it can be exploited

- The attack vector is LOCAL, so the attacker needs to get a malicious DjVu file onto the target system or into a pipeline where ExifTool will process it.
- No privileges and no user interaction are required, so any automated workflow that passes uploaded files through ExifTool could trigger the flaw without anyone clicking or approving anything.
- Public exploit code and write-ups exist showing this vulnerability being used against GitLab servers, where ExifTool was called automatically on uploaded images.
- Confidentiality, integrity and availability are all rated LOW in the CVSS score, but the description confirms arbitrary code execution is possible, so the practical impact on a given system could be significant depending on the permissions ExifTool runs with.

## What action to take

- Check whether any system or pipeline uses ExifTool version 7.44 or later and has not been updated to a version that includes the fix.
- The ExifTool maintainer published a commit that addresses the issue, linked in the references below.
- Debian and Fedora have issued their own advisories with patched packages, so if you run ExifTool from a distribution package manager you should update through that channel.
- Pay particular attention to any service that automatically processes uploaded files with ExifTool, since those can be reached without user interaction.
